Although they are different in nature, both can be seen as important historical stages and development foundations of their own civilizations.

The Alexander Empire was an empire established by Alexander the Great, the king of ancient Macedonia. Both represent the powerful countries and regional hegemony of their own civilizations.

background.source: Ancient Asia was the birthplace of several civilizations that developed around the fertile river valleys. These civilizations included Mesopotamia, India, and China, and they shared similarities and exchanged technologies and ideas such as mathematics and the wheel. Mesopotamia gave the world the Code of Hammurabi and the use of cuneiform, while the Persian Empire rose to a powerful position in the region. Judaism also has its roots in ancient Asia, developing in the Middle East. The spread of Islam in later centuries gave rise to the Islamic Golden Age and influenced the age of Islamic gunpowder empires. The history of Asia also includes major developments such as the trade of the Silk Road and the innovation of gunpowder, which not only affected Asia but also had a significant impact on other parts of the world.
background.target: Ancient Greece was a civilization that existed from the Greek Dark Ages of the 12th-9th centuries BC until the end of classical antiquity. Comprising a loose collection of culturally and linguistically related city-states and other territories, Ancient Greece formed most of these regions officially only once, under Alexander the Great's empire. Western history saw the era of classical antiquity immediately followed by the Early Middle Ages and the Byzantine period. With the archaic and classical periods forming a significant time, Greek urban poleis began to form in the 8th century BC, ushering in the colonization of the Mediterranean Basin. The Golden Age of Athens followed the Greco-Persian Wars until the 5th to 4th centuries BC. Alexander the Great’s conquests spread Hellenistic civilization from the western Mediterranean to Central Asia. Classical Greek culture, especially philosophy, had a significant influence on ancient Rome, which carried a version of it throughout the Mediterranean and much of Europe. Thus, Classical Greece is generally considered the cradle of Western civilization, the seminal culture from which the modern West derives many founding archetypes and ideas in politics, philosophy, science, and art.
